title: Hamiltonian Cycle
body:
A cycle in a [[Graph]] that visits **every vertex exactly once** and returns to where it
started. Asking whether a given graph has one is the first problem in the course with no
known efficient answer: it is [[NP-Complete]].

A *Hamiltonian path* is the same thing without the return trip. Both are hard.

```
A --- B        A -> B -> D -> C -> A   visits all four, returns to A
|  X  |        so this graph is Hamiltonian
C --- D
```

## Why it is hard

There is no local rule. Whether an edge belongs in the cycle depends on the entire rest of
the graph, so the obvious algorithm is to try every ordering of the vertices and check:
$O(n!)$. Backtracking prunes the search and helps enormously in practice, but the worst case
is still exponential, and after decades nobody has found a polynomial algorithm. Verifying a
proposed cycle, on the other hand, is trivially $O(V)$: walk it and tick off vertices. That
gap between "hard to find, easy to check" is the definition of NP.

## The near-miss

Compare an **Eulerian** circuit, which uses every *edge* exactly once instead of every
vertex. That one has a one-line test: a connected graph has an Eulerian circuit exactly when
every vertex has even degree. Two problems that sound almost identical, one solved by
counting and one open, which is a good illustration that the difficulty of a problem is not
predictable from how it is phrased.

Travelling salesman is the [[Weighted Graph]] version: not just "is there a Hamiltonian
cycle" but "which is cheapest", and it is at least as hard.
